title: Short Video Trends: What Will Land This Year
meta_description: We break down this year's short video trends: which formats work now, what's outdated, and how to adapt trends to your niche.
og_description: Which short video formats actually work right now, and how to tell a trend from a passing fad.

sections.h2: Why chasing every trend is a bad strategy

blocks.text: A trend built on someone else's sound or transition lives anywhere from a few days to a couple of weeks. By the time you've noticed it, come up with an idea for it, and filmed it, the algorithm is already showing the next one. Chasing every micro-trend drains your energy and rarely brings steady growth.

A more workable approach is to look not at the specific sounds and transitions, but at the type of content they serve. Trends come and go, while the format behind them often sticks around for a long time.
A few directions have stayed effective for several seasons now, changing only their outer wrapping.

rows: Viewers find it more interesting to watch something being made than to see the finished outcome
Honest breakdowns of your own mistakes
Builds more trust than videos with a perfect picture
Talking to the camera without editing
Feels livelier than videos overloaded with effects
Answering a comment with a separate video
Shows a dialogue with your audience and hands you a ready topic

blocks.text: The overall direction is that viewers increasingly choose what looks human over what looks polished. Overly smooth editing sometimes works against a video rather than for it.

sections.h2: What's clearly going out of style

items: Directly copying someone else's trend without adapting it to your niche
Overloaded editing with effects for the sake of effects
Clickbait titles that the video itself never delivers on
The same video structure for months without a single change

blocks.text: An audience quickly notices when a format is used mechanically, with no connection to the content. That doesn't mean trends aren't needed at all - it means you should filter them for your topic rather than grabbing them all in a row.

sections.h2: How to adapt a trend to your niche

blocks.text: Look at the mechanics, not the picture

Before you repeat someone else's video, figure out why it worked: an unexpected twist, honesty, a specific benefit. Then carry that exact principle over to your topic, not just the sound or transition.
Test a trend on a small scale

You don't have to rebuild your whole strategy around one noticeable trend. Film one or two videos in the new format and compare them with your usual numbers - if the result is noticeably better, it's worth continuing.

I stopped running after every new sound and started asking myself: what exactly holds attention here? It turned out that with my audience it's not the transition that lands, it's honesty on camera - and that's been working for half a year now, not a week.

sections.h2: Where to look so you don't miss trends

blocks.text: You don't need to scroll the feed for hours hunting for ideas. It's enough to browse the recommendations section in your niche every few days and notice recurring techniques across different creators - if the same principle shows up with several bloggers in a row, that's a signal, not a coincidence.
It's also useful to watch your own stats: sometimes your personal 'trend' that lands specifically with your audience is more valuable than a general platform trend.

faq.q: Should I repeat a trend if it doesn't fit my niche?
faq.a: It's better to adapt the trend's principle to your topic than to repeat it literally. Direct copying with no connection to the content usually delivers no result.

faq.q: How quickly do I need to react to a new trend?
faq.a: A fast reaction matters for trends tied to a specific sound or transition, but format shifts, like honesty on camera, can be adopted calmly and without rushing.

faq.q: Can I build content only on durable formats and ignore the fads?
faq.a: You can, and it's a workable strategy. Durable formats give a steady result, while individual trends can be used selectively, when they naturally fit the topic.

faq.q: How do I know a trend is already outdated?
faq.a: If you see it everywhere and it has started showing up on large accounts outside your niche, the peak has most likely passed and it's too late to jump in.

faq.q: Do I need to give up trends for the sake of my own style?
faq.a: Not entirely. Your own style and trends don't rule each other out - you can run a trend through your own voice instead of copying it one to one.
